history.heading: Arctic islands
paragraphs: Svalbard is an Arctic archipelago between mainland Norway and the North Pole; Jan Mayen is a separate volcanic island in the North Atlantic. Dutch explorer Willem Barentsz sighted Svalbard in 1596. Whalers from many nations hunted there in the 17th and 18th centuries, and Russian Pomors hunted and trapped.

Coal mining began in the early 20th century. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty gave Norway sovereignty but allowed citizens of all signatory countries to live and conduct business there. Russia continues to operate a coal mining settlement at Barentsburg. Jan Mayen became part of Norway in 1930.

culture.heading: Life in the high Arctic
paragraphs: About 2,500 people live in Svalbard, mostly in Longyearbyen, one of the world's northernmost towns, with residents from dozens of countries. Polar bears outnumber people, and residents carry rifles outside towns. The sun does not set from April to August, and polar night lasts from November to January. Jan Mayen has only a small staff of military and weather station personnel.

politics.heading: Norwegian territory
paragraphs: Svalbard is part of Norway, administered by a governor (sysselmester), with a local council in Longyearbyen. Under the treaty, it is demilitarised. Jan Mayen is administered from mainland Norway.

economy.heading: From coal to research
paragraphs: Coal mining is being phased out. The economy now relies on tourism, scientific research (including the University Centre in Svalbard) and satellite ground stations. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores backup copies of the world's crop seeds. There is no VAT, and taxes are low. The currency is the Norwegian krone.
